Lorentz Force. The combined electric and magnetic force exerted on a charged particle by electromagnetic fields. Formulated mathematically by Dutch physicist Hendrik Lorentz in the 1890s, it unifies the separate phenomena of electric and magnetic forces into a single relativistically invariant law: F equals q times E plus v cross B, where the electric field E exerts a force independent of motion, while the magnetic field B exerts a velocity-dependent force. The Lorentz force is the foundation of classical electromagnetism and explains the motion of charged particles in accelerators, plasma confinement, auroras, and countless other phenomena.

The electric-field component F subscript E equals q E acts on any charge, whether moving or stationary, in the direction parallel or antiparallel to the field. The magnetic-field component F subscript B equals q v cross B acts only on moving charges and is perpendicular to both velocity and field. A stationary charge experiences no magnetic force.

The cross product v cross B means the magnetic force depends on the angle between velocity and field: maximum when perpendicular, zero when parallel, creating circular or helical paths. A charged particle in a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to its velocity follows a circular arc with radius r equals m v divided by q B and cyclotron frequency f equals q B divided by two pi m.

This principle powers cyclotrons, accelerators where charged particles spiral in controlled paths to gain energy, and magnetrons, microwave generators. The Lorentz force explains why compasses align with Earth's magnetic field and why the auroras glow. Solar wind particles spiral along the magnetic field lines near the poles. In plasma physics, the Lorentz force on ions and electrons collectively determines plasma behavior, confinement, and instabilities in fusion reactors.

The force is frame-dependent. An electric force in one reference frame appears partly magnetic in another moving frame, revealing that E and B are aspects of a single relativistic electromagnetic field tensor.

The magnetic field is the source of one component of the Lorentz force. Electromagnetism is the broader framework unifying electric and magnetic phenomena through the Lorentz force. The electric field is the source of the other component. Velocity is the term determining the magnitude and direction of the magnetic-force component. Spin is an intrinsic angular momentum of particles that experiences a magnetic-force-like interaction called magnetic moment in external fields.
